capstone: Capstone: build an 'employee data services' PL/SQL package on Oracle Database Free (23ai Free). Generate a 5,000-row practice table yourself, then deliver a package spec/body that: (1) loads and transforms the data using BULK COLLECT with LIMIT plus FORALL, (2) exposes at least one procedure with IN/OUT parameters and one function callable from SQL, (3) implements structured error handling with a persistent error-log table, a user-defined exception, and RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR for business-rule violations, (4) keeps private helpers hidden in the package body. Include a one-page performance memo with measured timings (DBMS_UTILITY.GET_TIME) comparing your bulk implementation against a row-by-row version of the same task, and a short README explaining each design choice. Everything must run with free tools only (SQL*Plus or SQLcl against 23ai Free); no paid license required.
disclaimer: Original study guide keyed to public curriculum; course content itself lives at the source.

checkpoints: Which two sections of a block are optional, and what happens if the EXCEPTION section is absent when an error occurs?
Predict the output of a nested block where the inner block redeclares the outer block's variable with a different value.
Why does DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE appear to do nothing until you run SET SERVEROUTPUT ON?
An unhandled exception is raised in the inner block of two nested blocks, and neither has an exception section. Where does execution end up?
keyConcepts: Anonymous block vs named program unit
DECLARE section (optional): declarations
BEGIN: the mandatory executable section
EXCEPTION section (optional): error handlers
END: closing the block
Nested blocks and variable scope/shadowing
DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE for observable output
SET SERVEROUTPUT ON in SQL*Plus/SQLcl
labs: Hello-block run: write an anonymous block that prints a greeting with DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE. Run it with SET SERVEROUTPUT OFF, then ON, and note exactly what changes. (Oracle Database Free 23ai Free, free container or local install; connect with SQL*Plus or SQLcl — no paid license needed.)

Section drill: write a block with a DECLARE section containing a counter, loop from 1 to 5, and print each value. Then rewrite it so all work happens without a DECLARE section and describe what you had to give up.

Scope experiment: declare v_msg in an outer block, then redeclare v_msg with a different value in a nested inner block. Print v_msg inside the inner block and again after it ends; explain the shadowing you observe.

Exception flow trace: write a block that prints 'before', then performs 1/0, then prints 'after', with an exception section that prints 'handled'. Run it and map the exact execution order to the block structure.
objectives: Describe the DECLARE / BEGIN / EXCEPTION / END sections of a PL/SQL block and identify which are optional.
Execute anonymous blocks in SQL*Plus or SQLcl against Oracle Database Free (23ai Free) and observe output via DBMS_OUTPUT.
Predict variable scope and shadowing behavior in nested blocks.
Trace execution flow when an exception interrupts a block.
modules.title: Anonymous Blocks and Block Structure

checkpoints: What is the practical difference between v_name employees.last_name%TYPE and v_emp employees%ROWTYPE?
A DBA widens a VARCHAR2 column from 30 to 100 characters. Which declarations break, and which survive untouched?
Why is BOOLEAN legal in PL/SQL logic but not directly usable in a SQL statement?
When would you add NOT NULL or a DEFAULT to a declaration, and what risk does each remove?
keyConcepts: Scalar datatypes: VARCHAR2, NUMBER, DATE, BOOLEAN
NOT NULL and DEFAULT constraints on declarations
%TYPE: anchoring a variable to a column's datatype
%ROWTYPE: anchoring a record to a table or cursor row
Anchored declarations surviving schema changes
BOOLEAN as a PL/SQL-only datatype
CONSTANT declarations
Implicit conversion pitfalls between SQL and PL/SQL types
labs: Anchor lab: create your own small table lab_emp (emp_id NUMBER, first_name VARCHAR2(50), salary NUMBER). Declare variables anchored with lab_emp.first_name%TYPE and lab_emp%ROWTYPE, insert a row, fetch it back, and print the fields.

Resilience check: ALTER TABLE lab_emp to widen first_name to VARCHAR2(200). Re-run your previous block unchanged and confirm it still compiles and runs; then write the same logic with a hardcoded VARCHAR2(50) and show the contrast.
Record drill: fetch an entire lab_emp row into a %ROWTYPE record with SELECT ... INTO, then print three of its fields with DBMS_OUTPUT.

Boolean boundary: write a function-style block that computes a BOOLEAN flag (e.g., salary > 100000) and uses it in IF logic. Then try to SELECT that BOOLEAN into SQL and document the error you get and why it is expected.
objectives: Declare scalar variables with appropriate datatypes, NOT NULL constraints, and defaults.
Anchor declarations to table columns with %TYPE and to whole rows with %ROWTYPE.
Explain why anchored declarations are resilient to schema changes.
Choose between PL/SQL datatypes deliberately, including the limits of BOOLEAN.
modules.title: Variables, %TYPE, and %ROWTYPE

checkpoints: List the implicit cursor attributes and state what each one tells you after an UPDATE.
What three cursor operations does a cursor FOR loop perform for you automatically?
You need to run the same query twice with different department ids. Which cursor form fits best and why?
After OPEN, FETCH in a loop, and CLOSE: which step is most commonly forgotten, and what is the consequence?
keyConcepts: Implicit cursors and their attributes: SQL%ROWCOUNT, SQL%FOUND, SQL%NOTFOUND, SQL%ISOPEN
Explicit cursor lifecycle: DECLARE, OPEN, FETCH, CLOSE
Cursor FOR loops: implicit open, fetch, and close
Parameterized cursors
Loop records anchored with cursor%ROWTYPE
SELECT ... INTO as a single-row implicit cursor operation
Cursor FOR UPDATE and WHERE CURRENT OF for safe row locking
labs: Rowcount lab: populate lab_emp with 10 rows across two departments. Run an UPDATE that gives everyone in one department a raise, then print SQL%ROWCOUNT and branch on SQL%FOUND to print a confirmation message.

Explicit cursor walk: declare an explicit cursor over lab_emp ordered by emp_id; OPEN it, FETCH in a loop printing each name, then CLOSE it. Deliberately comment out the CLOSE once, re-run, and describe what you observe about cursor hygiene.
FOR loop conversion: rewrite the previous walk as a cursor FOR loop. Count the lines of both versions and note which cursor operations disappeared.
Parameterized cursor: declare a cursor that takes p_dept_id, then call it once per department in a loop, printing a header per department. Confirm the same cursor definition serves both calls.
objectives: Read implicit cursor attributes (SQL%ROWCOUNT, SQL%FOUND, SQL%NOTFOUND) after DML and single-row queries.
Implement the full explicit cursor lifecycle: declare, open, fetch in a loop, close.
Replace manual cursor code with cursor FOR loops where appropriate.
Parameterize cursors and select the right loop form for a given task.
modules.title: Cursors: Implicit, Explicit, and FOR Loops

checkpoints: What can an IN parameter do that an OUT parameter cannot, and vice versa?
A function you want to call from a SELECT statement has an OUT parameter and performs an INSERT. What two problems does that create?
What is the difference between positional and named notation when calling a subprogram, and when is named notation worth the verbosity?
Your function fails compilation. Which two data dictionary views or commands show you the exact error lines?
keyConcepts: CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE and FUNCTION
Parameter modes: IN, OUT, IN OUT
RETURN clause and RETURN statement in functions
Calling functions from SQL vs from PL/SQL
Positional vs named parameter notation
SHOW ERRORS and USER_ERRORS for compilation diagnostics
Dependency invalidation and recompilation
Default parameter values
labs: Procedure build: write give_raise(p_emp_id IN NUMBER, p_pct IN NUMBER) that updates lab_emp. Call it from an anonymous block, then verify the new salary with a SELECT.
Function in SQL: write annual_salary(p_emp_id IN NUMBER) RETURN NUMBER. Call it in a SELECT against lab_emp and in a PL/SQL assignment; confirm both work.
Break-and-fix: introduce a bad column name into annual_salary, attempt to compile, run SHOW ERRORS, read the exact line/column reported, fix it, and recompile cleanly.
OUT parameter drill: write get_dept_stats(p_dept_id IN NUMBER, p_headcount OUT NUMBER, p_avg_sal OUT NUMBER) that fills both OUT values with aggregate queries. Call it and print the results.
objectives: Create stored procedures and functions with IN, OUT, and IN OUT parameters.
Call functions from both SQL statements and PL/SQL blocks, respecting side-effect rules.
Diagnose compilation failures with SHOW ERRORS and the USER_ERRORS view.
Apply parameter design basics: modes, defaults, and calling notations.
modules.title: Stored Procedures and Functions

checkpoints: Which parts of a package must appear in the specification, and which may live only in the body?
You change only the package body. Do dependent procedures invalidate? What if you change the spec instead?
Where would you put a helper that formats log messages for internal use only, and why?
A package-level counter keeps its value between your calls in one session but resets in a new session. What does that tell you about package state?
keyConcepts: Package specification: the public interface
Package body: implementation and private items
Public vs private procedures, functions, and variables
Package-level state and session persistence
Initialization section of a package body
Forward declarations within a body
Spec-change vs body-change invalidation behavior
Grouping related subprograms into a cohesive API
labs: Package build: create package emp_admin with a spec declaring hire_emp, terminate_emp, and give_raise, plus a body implementing them against lab_emp. Add a private procedure log_action visible only inside the body and call it from each public routine.

Session state: add a package-level variable g_hire_count incremented by hire_emp. Call hire_emp three times in one session and print the counter; open a second session and print it again. Document the difference.

Invalidation experiment: recompile only the package body with a changed log message and confirm dependent callers stay valid. Then add a new parameter to a spec procedure and observe which dependents invalidate.
Privacy check: from outside the package, try to call the private log_action directly. Record the exact error and explain what it proves about encapsulation.
objectives: Separate a package's public interface (specification) from its implementation (body).
Group related procedures and functions behind a single package API with shared private state.
Keep helper routines private to the package body using encapsulation.
Explain how spec changes versus body changes affect dependent objects.
modules.title: Packages: Specification and Body

checkpoints: Contrast associative arrays, nested tables, and VARRAYs: how is each indexed, and can it be stored in a database column?
Why does BULK COLLECT usually carry a LIMIT clause, and what goes wrong without one on a million-row table?
Rewrite this in your head: a FOR loop that UPDATEs one row per iteration. What does the FORALL version look like?
After a FORALL with SAVE EXCEPTIONS, how do you find out which rows failed and why?
keyConcepts: Associative arrays (INDEX BY tables)
Nested tables
VARRAYs and their fixed maximum size
BULK COLLECT for multi-row fetches
LIMIT clause to bound memory use
FORALL for bulk DML over collections
SQL%BULK_ROWCOUNT for per-statement row counts
SAVE EXCEPTIONS and SQL%BULK_EXCEPTIONS
labs: Associative array: declare TYPE t_ids IS TABLE OF NUMBER INDEX BY PLS_INTEGER; load it with employee ids from lab_emp in a loop, then iterate and print them. Note the sparse-index behavior if you skip an index.
Bulk fetch: build a 500-row staging table, then BULK COLLECT into a nested table with LIMIT 100 inside a loop, printing the batch count each pass until done.

Speed comparison: time a row-by-row UPDATE loop over 5,000 rows with DBMS_UTILITY.GET_TIME, then time the equivalent FORALL UPDATE over a BULK COLLECTed collection. Record both timings and the speedup factor.

Graceful bulk errors: seed one bad row (e.g., a duplicate key) into a FORALL INSERT with SAVE EXCEPTIONS; after it runs, loop over SQL%BULK_EXCEPTIONS and print each failing index with its error code.
objectives: Declare and use associative arrays, nested tables, and VARRAYs, stating the differences.
Fetch multi-row result sets efficiently with BULK COLLECT, bounding memory with LIMIT.
Apply DML across collections with FORALL instead of row-by-row loops.
Combine BULK COLLECT and FORALL to eliminate slow-by-slow processing.
modules.title: Collections and Bulk Binds (BULK COLLECT / FORALL)

checkpoints: RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR is called with -19999. What is wrong, and what range is legal?
Your block has WHEN DUP_VAL_ON_INDEX, then WHEN OTHERS. A unique violation occurs. Which handler runs, and why does order matter?
You catch WHEN OTHERS, print a message, and do nothing else. Name two concrete harms of this pattern.
An exception raised in a procedure with no handler: describe its propagation path to the caller.
keyConcepts: Exception section structure and handler order
Predefined exceptions: NO_DATA_FOUND, TOO_MANY_ROWS, DUP_VAL_ON_INDEX, ZERO_DIVIDE
User-defined exceptions: declaration, RAISE, handling
RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR and the -20000..-20999 range
SQLCODE and SQLERRM for diagnostics
EXCEPTION_INIT pragma for naming Oracle error numbers
Exception propagation across call stacks
WHEN OTHERS: log and re-raise, never swallow
labs: Predefined catch: write a block that SELECTs a nonexistent emp_id INTO a variable. Catch NO_DATA_FOUND and print a friendly message instead of letting the raw error surface.
User-defined rule: declare e_raise_too_big EXCEPTION; in a raise procedure, RAISE it when p_pct > 20; handle it in the caller with a clear business message.

Application error: in a terminate_emp procedure, call RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR(-20001, 'Cannot terminate employee with active projects') when a rule fails. Catch it in the caller and print SQLCODE and SQLERRM.
Name an error: use PRAGMA EXCEPTION_INIT to associate e_dup_emp with ORA-00001, then attempt a duplicate emp_id insert and handle e_dup_emp specifically.

Honest OTHERS: build an error_log table; write a procedure whose WHEN OTHERS inserts SQLCODE/SQLERRM plus a timestamp into error_log and then re-raises with RAISE. Trigger it and verify both the log row and the propagated error.
objectives: Catch and handle predefined exceptions deliberately instead of letting raw errors surface.
Declare, raise, and handle user-defined exceptions for business rules.
Raise application errors with RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR inside the legal error-number range.
Write WHEN OTHERS handlers that log diagnostics and re-raise rather than swallowing errors.
modules.title: Exception Handling: Predefined, User-Defined, RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR

checkpoints: Define a SQL-to-PL/SQL context switch in one sentence and explain why thousands of them are expensive.
A report query is written as a cursor loop that prints one row at a time. What is the first rewrite you attempt before reaching for bulk binds?
Why do literal values in repeated SQL cause hard parses while bind variables allow soft parses?
You timed two approaches and the 'faster' one wins by 3% on 100 rows. What do you change about the experiment before trusting it?
keyConcepts: SQL/PL/SQL context switches and slow-by-slow processing
Set-based SQL as the first and cheapest rewrite
Bulk binds (BULK COLLECT/FORALL) as the second line of defense
Bind variables vs literals in the shared pool
Hard parse vs soft parse
Measuring with DBMS_UTILITY.GET_TIME
Row-by-row as the option of last resort
Documenting before/after timings for every optimization claim
labs: Set-based win: time a PL/SQL loop that inserts 10,000 rows one at a time with DBMS_UTILITY.GET_TIME; then time a single INSERT ... SELECT doing the same work. Record both numbers and the ratio.
Loop-to-SQL rewrite: take the cursor-loop UPDATE from the cursors module and rewrite it as one UPDATE statement; time both and note which is simpler to read as well as faster.
Bind variable demo: in a loop of 1,000 iterations, run EXECUTE IMMEDIATE with a concatenated literal once and with a bind variable once; time both and explain the gap in terms of parsing.
Optimization memo: pick any earlier lab that used row-by-row logic, rewrite it, and write a five-line memo stating the before/after timings, what you changed, and why the new version is faster.
objectives: Identify row-by-row (slow-by-slow) patterns and the context switches that make them expensive.
Rewrite row-by-row logic as set-based SQL first and bulk binds second.
Explain why bind variables reduce hard parsing in the shared pool.
Measure performance claims with timings instead of asserting them.
modules.title: Performance Basics: Avoiding Row-by-Row, Bind Variables

objectives: Set up Oracle Database Free (23ai Free) via its free container image or local install and connect with the free SQL*Plus or SQLcl clients; every lab in this sequence runs there with no paid license required.
Write, run, and debug the core PL/SQL building blocks: anonymous blocks, anchored variables, cursors, stored subprograms, and packages.
Handle errors deliberately with predefined exceptions, user-defined exceptions, and RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR, including persistent error logging.
Apply bulk SQL techniques (BULK COLLECT, FORALL) and performance basics (set-based rewrites, bind variables) to avoid slow-by-slow processing.
